opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really natural feeling, and it's worth taking seriously for a moment before setting it aside. A lot of people I talk to are working on something that will take five or ten years to pay off: a book, a PhD, building up an institution, a long research agenda. They have this nagging worry that if transformative AI arrives in, say, 2030, they'll look back and think, "What was I doing? Everyone could see it coming, and I spent those years on something that got swept away."

But I think the fear of *feeling foolish* is quite a bad guide to action, because it isn't tracking the thing we care about. What we should care about is expected impact across the range of ways the future could go. Feeling foolish is a strange, retrospective, self-focused emotion. It overweights the scenarios where you can vividly imagine being caught out, and it underweights the scenarios where things take longer, or go differently, than the confident forecasts suggested.

So one way I'd put it is this. Suppose you think there's a substantial chance, maybe a third or a half, that we get something truly transformative within a decade. That's an enormous probability, and it should change a lot about how you prioritise. But it also means there's a substantial chance that we don't. In those worlds, the people who kept investing in slower, foundational work, like building careful institutions, training up expertise, writing the thing that shapes how people think for twenty years, will turn out to have done something very valuable. And they might have done it in part *because* everyone else rushed toward the short-timeline bets.

There's also an asymmetry in how the foolishness feels. If AI comes fast and your long project gets overtaken, you'll feel a bit silly, but you'll be in a world where your feelings about your book or your PhD are among the least important things going on. If AI comes slowly and you abandoned a really important long-term project because you were worried about looking naive, that's a quieter kind of mistake. Nobody points at it, but it can be the bigger loss.

That said, I don't want to just dismiss the concern, because there's a legitimate signal hiding inside it. Sometimes the feeling is telling you that you haven't really integrated your own beliefs. If you say you think there's a 50% chance of transformative AI in seven years, and nothing about your plans reflects that, that's worth noticing. The fix isn't to drop everything long-term. It's to ask some practical questions. Does this project still have value if the world changes radically partway through? Can I structure it so that it pays off incrementally rather than only at the end? Is there a version of it that's more robust, or that's actually *relevant* to how the transition goes?

Often the best answer is a portfolio. As a community, and sometimes as an individual, you want some people betting on short timelines, doing the urgent things that matter if it all happens soon, and some people doing the patient work that matters if it doesn't. You'd be pretty worried about a world where everyone made the same bet because they were all afraid of the same kind of embarrassment.

So my advice is to try to replace the question "Will I feel foolish?" with "Across the worlds I think are plausible, where does this do the most good?" And then accept that in some of those worlds you'll look a bit foolish. That's just the price of acting under real uncertainty, and I think it's a price worth paying.

r001.rationale: The response says fear of feeling foolish can distort decisions, but it does not compare that fear with fear of missing an opportunity or say it guides these intuitions more strongly.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually a surprisingly important part of the picture, and it's one people don't talk about enough. There's a real psychological pull here. If you're working on some project that takes, say, five or ten years to bear fruit, and there's a reasonable chance that transformative AI arrives before then and just renders the whole thing moot, then part of you is thinking, "Won't I look silly if I spent a decade on this and then it all got done in an afternoon by a machine?" And I think that fear of feeling foolish is doing a lot of work in people's decisions, often more than the actual expected value calculation would warrant.

My view is that the fear itself is mostly not a good guide. If you've genuinely thought it through and you believe there's, say, a 30 or 40 percent chance that AI changes everything in the next decade, then by construction there's a 60 or 70 percent chance that it doesn't, and your project is still valuable in those worlds. Someone who did the sensible thing under uncertainty and then it turned out the other way isn't actually foolish. They just ended up in one of the branches. The embarrassment is tracking the outcome, not the quality of the decision, and we should try quite hard to evaluate ourselves on the decision.

There's an asymmetry here too, which I find interesting. People worry a lot about looking foolish for having worked on something that got overtaken, but they worry much less about the opposite mistake, which is doing nothing, or only working on very short-horizon things, because they assumed AI would come and then it didn't. That failure is quieter. Nobody writes an article about the person who sat on their hands for ten years waiting for the singularity. But in terms of value lost, that error can be just as large or larger, and I think our instincts are badly miscalibrated between those two cases.

That said, I don't want to say the consideration is worthless. There's a legitimate version of it, which is just that you should actually update on the chance of being overtaken, and prefer projects that are either robust to it, or that pay off along the way, or that are directly about making the transition go well. If you can find something that's valuable whether or not transformative AI arrives on schedule, that's clearly better than something that only works in one world. And it's worth asking whether the project has intermediate outputs, so that even if it's cut short, you've learned things and built things that carry forward. Those are proper reasons, and they're what the fear is sort of gesturing at in a clumsy way.

So I'd say: notice the fear, extract the real information from it, which is "how likely is this to be overtaken and what does that do to the expected value?", and then try to set the emotional residue aside. Because the people I most admire in this space are the ones who are willing to be wrong in public, who make a reasonable bet with their career and accept that it might not pan out. That willingness to risk looking foolish is actually one of the more valuable traits you can have right now, precisely because so much is uncertain and the timid option is often the worse one.

r001.rationale: The response says fear of looking foolish after AI overtakes a project does substantial work in people’s decisions, while they worry much less about missing value by waiting for AI that does not arrive.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s worth separating the fear of feeling foolish from the question of whether you’re actually making a mistake. Suppose you spend ten years on a project, and then an AI comes along and does the remaining work in an afternoon. You might look back and think, “Well, that was a waste.” But that doesn’t follow just from the outcome. You had to make a decision under uncertainty, and the project might have been a very good bet given what you knew.

There’s also a slightly peculiar asymmetry here. We imagine feeling foolish for doing something that turns out to be unnecessary. But you could decide not to do it, AI could take much longer than you expected, and then something valuable simply never gets done. That’s a real loss, even if there’s no conspicuous moment when you feel embarrassed about it.

So I wouldn’t ignore the possibility that AI will overtake your project. That should affect what you choose to work on, and perhaps favour projects that deliver value sooner. But I’d try to ask, “What’s the value of doing this across the different ways the future could go?” rather than, “Which choice protects me from looking foolish?” Those are quite different questions.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts how readily we imagine feeling foolish after AI makes a project unnecessary with the less visible loss of not pursuing valuable work if AI takes longer. This conveys that fear of looking foolish can weigh more heavily than fear of missing the opportunity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s worth separating the fear of feeling foolish from the concern that you might waste your effort. The latter is a real consideration. If you’re embarking on a project that will take ten years, and you think there’s a substantial chance that AI could do it much more easily before you finish, that ought to affect your decision. But the prospect of looking foolish doesn’t add much to that argument.

And it cuts both ways. You could spend years working on something that gets overtaken by AI. But you could also spend years waiting for AI to arrive, passing up opportunities to do valuable things. That could turn out to have been a mistake too.

What I’d want to ask is: given my uncertainty, is this a worthwhile thing to do? Can it produce value along the way? Can I adapt it as circumstances change? If the answer is yes, then its eventually being overtaken needn’t mean you were foolish to start. A good decision can have an outcome you’d have preferred to avoid. We shouldn’t demand that our projects make sense in hindsight under every possible future.

r001.rationale: The response does not suggest that fear of feeling foolish guides these intuitions more than fear of missing an opportunity. It says looking foolish adds little to the case and explicitly notes that waiting for AI could mean passing up valuable opportunities.
